name: Aaron Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Aaron. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties, and what you say is confidential. You can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. What does a normal day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at Brightwater, which is free-range eggs, three sheds of about four thousand hens each, plus wheat and oilseed rape on the rest. Morning is egg collection and checking the sheds, the feeders, the water, the dead ones, which you get used to. Afternoon I'm with Hugh, the manager, on whatever's going, and I'm still the guy who gets the trailer stuck at the gateway.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the gadgets, honestly. I use AI on my phone every day, I asked it to work out why shed two's laying dropped, and it was right, the lights were on the wrong timer. Hard part is money, I'm on the bottom rate, I share a house in Kelby with two lads from the meat plant, and I've got maybe three weeks saved. I spent the rest on a second-hand drone, which Hugh thinks was stupid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still a good tool, people just oversold it. I'd probably post a video of me using it to sort out the hens, like 'see, still useful'. I don't get into arguments online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, a bit disappointed, because I was betting on it. If it stays small, I'm still a junior on a poultry farm with not much going on. But I'd still use it to get better faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep using it every day, keep learning. I'd try to get Hugh to let me run the shed data, the temperatures and egg counts. And I'd start charging neighbours to fly the drone over their fields, maybe thirty a go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat, like a party that ended early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the drone for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Crop pictures, mostly. I fly it over the rape and you can see where the pigeons have been at it, or where it's waterlogged. Two farmers already asked me to do theirs, I did it for a coffee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing much changes, where do you see yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Running a farm's tech side, I hope. Or doing drone work for ten farms at once. Something where I'm the one people ring.

S0.say: It's still a good tool, people just oversold it. I'd post a video of me using it on the hens, like 'see, still useful', but I don't argue online.
S0.think: I'd be a bit disappointed, because I was betting on it. I'd still be a junior on a poultry farm, but I'd use it to get better faster.
S0.do: Keeps using AI daily and asks Hugh to let him run the shed data. Starts charging neighbours about thirty a flight for drone crop pictures.
S0.quote: Two farmers already asked me to do theirs, I did it for a coffee.
S0.fieldNote: Aaron is the tech-keen junior who'd find the plateau slightly disappointing. He already has the seed of a side business with his drone. He's practical and not political, more interested in being the person people call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say get on board, it's happening either way. Learn it now while it's new and you can be the expert. At the pub I'd be the one showing people the egg-counting app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's good for me, honestly. Robots in the sheds need someone to look after them, and I'm the only one under fifty who wants to. I'd probably end up with more responsibility, maybe more pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Hugh to send me on whatever training the robot company runs, and offer to do it on my day off. I'd keep growing the drone thing, maybe ten farms by the end of the year. I'd do an online course in farm robotics in the evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the farm would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steve, who's been here twenty years. He hates computers, and he's good at his job, but his job is walking the sheds. I'd try to help him, but I don't know if he'd let me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you pay for training on your money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Day off and evenings, and the drone money. If Brightwater paid for it, great, but I wouldn't wait for them. Most of the stuff I learn is free online anyway.

S1.say: Get on board, it's happening either way. Learn it now while it's new and you can be the expert.
S1.think: It's good for me, honestly. Robots in the sheds need looking after, and I'm the only one under fifty who wants to, so I'd likely get more responsibility and maybe more pay.
S1.do: Asks Hugh to send him on the robot company's training, using his day off if needed, and takes an evening online course in farm robotics. Grows the drone work to about ten farms by the end of the year.
S1.quote: I'm the only one under fifty who wants to.
S1.fieldNote: Steady disruption looks like an opportunity to Aaron, and his thin savings don't stop him because most of what he learns is free. His one worry is for Steve, a long-serving colleague who walks the sheds. He'd act first, without waiting for the farm to pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is huge and nobody's ready, me included. I'd tell people not to wait for the government, because they won't be quick enough. I'd say look after each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, two years is too fast for me to get ahead. If the AI can do everything, it can fly the drone and fix the robots itself. I'd have about a year of being useful, then I'm just another guy with no job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make as much from the drone as I can, fast, while farmers still need someone. I'd cut back on everything else, sell the gaming PC. I'd look for whatever job is left, maybe installing the robots for a dealer. If there was a government scheme, I'd take it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Really anxious, but I'd be busy, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said in the slower one you'd be the expert. Does that still work here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Being the expert only works if the machines need a person. In two years they don't. I'd be like the guy who learned to fix fax machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the money look like, month to month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight. Rent's the big one, and the drone money would come and go. If it goes bad, I'd move back to my mum's, she's got my old room. Not proud of that, but it's there.

S2.say: This is huge and nobody's ready, me included. Don't wait for the government, because they won't be quick enough, and look after each other.
S2.think: Two years is too fast for me to get ahead. If the AI can fly the drone and fix the robots itself, I'd have about a year of being useful before I'm just another guy with no job.
S2.do: Earns as much as possible from drone work while it lasts and cuts spending, selling his gaming PC. Looks for robot installation work with a dealer and could move back to his mum's if money runs out.
S2.feel: Really anxious, but busy, which helps.
S2.quote: I'd be like the guy who learned to fix fax machines.
S2.fieldNote: Aaron's confidence depends on machines still needing a person, and two years removes that. He stays active rather than frozen, which keeps him at anxious rather than alarmed. His mum's spare room is his quiet safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so let's be clever about it. Learn the tools, build something. I'd show people what I'm doing on the drone side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years is a real window. I'd be the one setting up robots on farms round here for a few years, and I'd make money doing it. At the end it might not need me, but I'd have savings and contacts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd do a proper robotics certificate and register the drone business properly. I'd try to save a bit from every job, maybe a fifth. I'd also learn the AI tools that run farm robots, because that's where the work would be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. More excited than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you do with years three to five, once you see it coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to move up the chain, from fixing the machines to setting up whole systems for farms. Then maybe to whoever manages them across a region. Each step buys a bit more time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay at Brightwater?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a year or two, to learn their robots. Then I'd go out on my own, or with a dealer. Hugh would understand, he did the same when he was young.

S3.say: We've got a few years, so let's be clever about it. Learn the tools, build something, and I'll show people what I'm doing on the drone side.
S3.think: Five years is a real window. I'd spend a few years setting up robots on local farms and make money doing it, so even if it ends up not needing me, I'd have savings and contacts.
S3.do: Takes a proper robotics certificate and registers his drone business. Saves about a fifth of every job and learns the AI tools that run farm robots.
S3.quote: Each step buys a bit more time.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives Aaron a plan to climb from fixing machines to setting up systems and then managing them regionally. He sees each step as buying time rather than a final answer. He'd leave Brightwater on good terms after learning the robots there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, get skilled up and you'll be fine for most of it. I'd tell the young lads at the plant to learn the machines now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd do well for eight years, maybe nine. Robots spread slowly at first, and I'd be ahead. The end point's the same, but I'd have built something by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, the robotics certificate, the drone business, and I'd buy a second, better drone with what I save. I'd go to the farm shows to meet dealers. I'd learn the AI side every day, like I already do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit. Mostly hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra time do to your own life plans, outside work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want my own place, not a shared house. Maybe a girlfriend who doesn't mind me talking about drones. Ten years gives me time to actually get that, which two years doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that could go wrong with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get comfortable. That's my risk, being too pleased with myself. If I'm doing well in year five, I might forget it all ends the same way.

S4.say: Ten years is a long time, so get skilled up and you'll be fine for most of it. Young lads should learn the machines now.
S4.think: I'd do well for eight or nine years, because robots spread slowly at first and I'd be ahead. The end point's the same, but I'd have built something by then.
S4.do: Takes the robotics certificate, grows the drone business and buys a second, better drone with savings. Goes to farm shows to meet dealers and keeps learning AI daily.
S4.feel: A little uneasy, but mostly hopeful.
S4.quote: If I'm doing well in year five, I might forget it all ends the same way.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years is Aaron's best case, giving him time to build a business and a personal life. He's honest that his risk is complacency rather than fear. He invests his small savings in equipment rather than keeping cash.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'd be learning stuff that's out of date before I finish. What would help is cheap loans for young people starting businesses, and some money to live on while you switch, so you don't have to sell your drone to pay rent.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what happens to the hens. If robots run the sheds, who decides when a hen's suffering? I'm into tech, but I've seen what happens when nobody's looking.

headlineQuote: I'm into tech, but I've seen what happens when nobody's looking.
portrait: Aaron Torres is 27, the junior hand at Brightwater, a free-range egg and arable farm, sharing a house in Kelby with about three weeks of savings and a second-hand drone. He uses AI every day and is already earning a little from drone crop pictures for neighbours. He is calm in the plateau and steady disruption, seeing robots as his chance to become the farm's tech person. Only AGI in two years makes him anxious, because the machines would no longer need him. With five or ten years he plans to climb from fixing robots to setting up whole systems, while admitting his risk is getting comfortable.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because whatever he learned would be out of date before he finished.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap loans for young people starting businesses, and money to live on while switching work.
